# Money and finances 

Most of the money that pays for the Church of England’s ministry and mission comes from people who give to their local church. This page explains where the money comes from, who looks after it and what it pays for.

## Where the money comes from

Your local church’s ministry and mission is paid for mainly by the incredible generosity of local people who give to it regularly and through one-off gifts.

Churches and the wider Church of England also get money from:

- grants and fundraising for particular projects
- renting out buildings and other local income
- fees for weddings and funerals
- income from the Church's investments and land.

There is no single national pot that pays for everything. Money is held and spent at different levels, from the local church up to national bodies, and each level has its own responsibilities. 

## What your local church pays for

Your local church meets its own running costs. These include heating, lighting, insurance, and looking after the building. It pays for them mainly through giving from its congregation and local community. 

## Parish Share

Every parish is asked to give money to its diocese so that it can support parish ministry throughout the diocese. This is called the Parish Share. Some dioceses call it by other names such as the Common Fund or the Diocesan Share.

Parish Share pays for most of the cost of ministry in parishes, including:

- clergy pay, known as stipends
- housing for clergy
- training
- pension contributions for clergy serving now
- the diocesan staff who support parishes.

Parish Share contributions go to the diocese, not to the national Church. Dioceses manage the process in different ways, but the aim is that each parish gives generously to a shared fund to support ministry across the diocese as a whole. 

## The Church’s national endowment fund

The Church Commissioners for England looks after the Church's national endowment fund. It is made up of money, land and property built up over many centuries.

The fund is invested to support the mission and ministry of the Church of England, today and for future generations. It is a historic fund and receives very little new money, so the Church Commissioners manages it carefully to make it last, and aims to grow what it provides in line with rising costs.

At the end of 2025 the fund was worth £11.6 billion. Each year it provides around a fifth of the funding needed for the work of the Church of England.

The fund is separate from parish giving. Money you give to your local church stays with your church and your diocese.

The Church Commissioners for England

## What national funding pays for

Every three years the Church Commissioners and the Archbishops' Council decide how much of the endowment income will be distributed and what it should support. For 2026 to 2028 they plan to distribute more than £1.6 billion. This is the largest distribution in the Church's history and 36 per cent more than for 2023 to 2025.

This money supports:

- dioceses and local churches, with extra help for the lowest income communities
- the work of bishops and archbishops
- cathedrals
- pensions for clergy who served before 1998, and retirement housing
- national programmes, such as work to reach net zero carbon and the national redress scheme for victims and survivors of abuse.

National funding does not pay for stipends directly. The Church Commissioners runs the national clergy ‘payroll’ with the funds for paying the clergy who serve in parishes coming from dioceses from Parish Share contributions and other sources. National funding helps dioceses to meet that cost, especially in the lowest income communities. 

Most of this money reaches dioceses and national programmes through the Archbishops' Council.

## What dioceses pay for

Dioceses use the Parish Share, their own investment income and national funding to pay for the clergy who serve in parishes. This covers stipends, housing and pension contributions for current service.

Dioceses also employ the staff who advise parishes on mission, buildings, safeguarding and legal and financial matters.

## Clergy pensions

Who pays for a member of clergy's pension depends on when they served:

- The Church Commissioners pays in full for pensions earned up to the end of 1997.
- The Church of England Funded Pensions Scheme pays pensions earned from 1 January 1998. This scheme is funded through contributions from dioceses and other church bodies.

The Church of England Pensions Board runs the pension schemes for clergy and lay employees of the Church and provides retirement housing for people who have served the Church. It also provides financial wellbeing services to help clergy prepare for retirement.

The Church of England Pensions Board

## Government funding

Churches get little direct government funding for their day-to-day work. Giving and other local income pays for the work of ministry and mission.

The Government does help with repairs to listed church buildings, and this help has recently changed. The Listed Places of Worship Grant Scheme, which gave churches grants matching the VAT they paid on repairs, closed on 31 March 2026.

In England it has been replaced by the Places of Worship Renewal Fund. This is a £92 million scheme over four years run by Historic England, which gives grants of between £10,000 and £1 million. Priority goes to buildings in the areas of greatest need.
